passages.happening:
Psalm 148 calls the whole universe to praise, starting at the top. “Hallelujah! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places” (verse 1). “Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts” (verse 2). “Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars” (verse 3). Even the highest heavens and the waters above the skies are called (verse 4).

The reason: “Let them praise the name of the LORD, for He gave the command and they were created” (verse 5). “He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The psalm moves in two great sweeps, like the opening of Genesis: first the heavens (verses 1 to 6), then the earth (verses 7 to 14). “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).

Many peoples around Israel worshipped the sun, the moon and the stars as gods. Psalm 148 turns them into worshippers. They are not gods to be praised. They are creatures that praise.

‘The waters above the skies’ (verse 4) is how the Hebrew Bible pictured the heavens, with waters above the sky, as in Genesis 1:7.

Verse 5 gives the reason in a few words. They exist because God spoke. That is enough reason to praise him.
passages.later: John saw every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea praising God and the Lamb: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!” (Revelation 5:13).
passages.asks:
Look up at the sky tonight. Psalm 148 says the sun, moon and stars are already praising God, simply by being what he made them to be. Their light is their praise.

You are invited to join a song that began long before you and fills the whole sky.

passages.t: ‘Praise the LORD from the earth’: sea creatures, snow, kings and children
passages.happening:
Now the call goes out across the earth. “Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths” (verse 7). Weather is called: “lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word” (verse 8). Then mountains and hills, fruit trees and cedars (verse 9), wild animals and cattle, creeping things and birds (verse 10).

Then people: “kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth” (verse 11), “young men and maidens, old and young together” (verse 12).

“Let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is exalted” (verse 13). The psalm ends with God's own people: “He has raised up a horn for His people, the praise of all His saints, of Israel, a people near to Him” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The great sea creatures and the deep (verse 7) were, for many ancient peoples, pictures of chaos and danger. Here they simply praise God along with everything else.

Notice the order of the list. It runs from the depths to the weather, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and then to people. Kings are not put at the top. They stand in line with young men and old women. Everyone, from the most powerful to the smallest child, owes the same praise.

A ‘horn’ was a picture of strength (see the note on Psalm 75). God has given his people strength, and given them a place near him. The ‘saints’ are God's faithful people.
passages.later:
Paul wrote that “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).

When the Pharisees told Jesus to quiet the crowds praising him, he said, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out” (Luke 19:40).
passages.asks:
Psalm 148 puts you in a choir with whales, hailstorms, cedar trees and kings. It is hard to feel too important, or too small, in that company.

How do you treat the rest of creation, if it too was made to praise God? And who in your life is ‘old’ or ‘young’ and needs to be invited to praise ‘together’?
